children: There's no easy fix for Social Security, but a plan to raise top earners' taxes has recently gained traction with lawmakers and the public.

The proposal isn't new, but it has gained fresh attention as Social Security's insolvency draws near. If Congress doesn't act, the retirement trust fund is projected to run dry in 2032, according to the latest estimates, triggering an automatic benefit cut of 22%.

Social Security's woes have worsened the country's debt burden, which recently hit $40 trillion. While the program is mostly self-financed through a dedicated payroll tax, in recent years it hasn't collected enough in revenue to cover promised benefits. That has forced the government to dip into the trust fund to make up the difference, redeeming its Treasury securities for cash and adding to the debt.
"The size of the problem is too big to ignore," says Karen E. Smith, senior fellow at the Urban Institute.

Lawmakers are finally starting to stir on the issue. Among other proposals, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D., Mass) and Sen. Bernie Moreno (R., Ohio) are working on legislation that would eliminate the payroll tax cap, which is $184,500 for 2026, the two wrote in a New York Times opinion piece this summer. Workers pay a 6.2% payroll tax-or 12.4% if they are self-employed-in Social Security taxes on earnings up to that amount.

Under this structure, the vast majority of Americans owe Social Security taxes on their entire paycheck. But the roughly 6% of earners whose wages exceed the cap every year owe money on just a portion of their earnings. And earnings at the top have grown faster than they have for average workers. Back in the early 1980s, about 90% of taxable earnings were subject to the cap, but today that has fallen to around 82%.

If the payroll cap had been nixed a decade ago, it would have closed Social Security's entire shortfall, says Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. But since the program didn't collect that extra revenue for 10 years, today the move would close only around two-thirds of the program's shortfall. That assumes that top earners were given no benefit credit for their additional wages taxed, according to the Social Security trustees.
"The longer we wait, the worse it'll be," MacGuineas says.

Killing the cap isn't the only option. In 2016, a commission convened by the Bipartisan Policy Center proposed lifting the cap so that it again covered 90% of wages. In 2026, that would mean a ceiling of $384,000 instead of $184,500, according to Social Security Administration actuaries. Other proposals would create a "doughnut hole," keeping the cap where it is and reinstating it above a certain threshold.

Much of the public supports some form of tax increases. Only 15% of respondents said that Social Security shouldn't raise taxes on any Americans, even if that meant benefit cuts, according to a poll last year by the National Academy of Social Insurance. Among Republicans, more than 75% preferred increasing revenue to benefit reductions, with higher support among Democrats and independents. The most popular proposal among respondents was reinstating the payroll cap at incomes above $400,000.

There are critics of such proposals, of course. They say lifting the cap would place an undue burden on higher earners and crowd out other priorities. Eliminating the cap would raise the marginal tax rate on wages for the highest-earning Americans to 60%-plus from the current 50%-plus, including federal and state income taxes and the 2.9% Medicare payroll tax, which doesn't have a cap, according to the right-leaning Manhattan Institute. A government can only tax so much, and such a move would use up most of the remaining "tax the rich" revenue in the service of already wealthy baby boomers, the institute said, leaving nothing for K-12 education, climate change, and other priorities.

But an analysis from the progressive Economic Policy Institute estimated that 70% of workers ages 32 to 66 who earned more than the taxable maximum in 2024 would lose more in Social Security benefits if the trust fund runs dry than they would pay in higher taxes if the cap were scrapped. The remaining 30% "includes politically influential multimillionaires and billionaires," the analysis noted.

Is there actually hope for a fix? Don't take this to the prediction markets, but Congress will probably wait until the last minute to pass a reform package that includes raising the full retirement age and raising the Social Security payroll tax cap.
